rationales.A: Background from the books: New York’s 1848 property law was one small gain; the vote and most other demands were still far from law.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Douglass rose to defend the suffrage resolution at Seneca Falls; his speech helped carry the only contested vote of the meeting.
rationales.C: Background from the books: when the one resolution that splits the room is the vote, and Douglass must rise to save it, suffrage stands out as the meeting’s boldest step.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the vote was discussed, debated, and passed; the debate itself is the point, not a refusal to discuss it.
rationales.general:
1. Count the fight: one resolution draws opposition while the others pass.
2. Background from the books: Douglass, the abolitionist editor, spoke for the vote and helped carry it.
3. Read what the split means: property and education were safer ground than the ballot in 1848.
Remember: the demand that divides even its friends is the one that marks the edge of its time.
